evidence: Travis — Texas A&M Travis County explicitly describes American persimmon as native to Travis County at the western edge of its range.
Williamson — historical cytogeographic collections include two Diospyros virginiana collections from Georgetown, Williamson County.
target_zone_range.blocking_issue: Only two exact target-zone counties are locked with adequate native/wild evidence in this pass.
target_zone_range.guardrail: Do not convert general eastern-Texas or Colorado-River range statements into unnamed counties.

morphology.look_here_first: Start with leaf size and fruit color. American persimmon has much larger leaves than Texas persimmon and ripe fruit is yellow-orange to reddish rather than black. Mature bark becomes dark and blocky rather than smooth, pale, and peeling.
diagnostic_traits: deciduous tree, often substantially taller than Texas persimmon
leaves typically much larger than D. texana
fruit larger and yellow-orange to reddish at maturity
fruit and mature leaves not densely tomentose like the Texas persimmon comparison

comparison.split: D. texana = small thick leaves with hairy undersides + smooth pale peeling bark + black fruit. D. virginiana = larger leaves + dark blocky bark + orange/red fruit.
